content.title: About
content.content: Quaker Chewy Granola Bar is a soft, chewy snack made from whole grains, honey, and dried fruit, produced by Quaker Oats. It is designed for a quick on‑the‑go bite and contains a blend of oats, sunflower seeds, raisins, and nuts, with a modest amount of sugar and salt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quaker Chewy bars are available in several flavors, such as chocolate, honey‑nut, and cranberry‑orange.
The product is marketed as an "energy snack" and is often promoted to athletes and active‑lifestyle consumers.
Each bar weighs about 35 g and provides roughly 150 kcal.
Quaker Oats is one of the oldest cereal brands in the United States, founded in 1901.
Bars contain no artificial colors, though some flavors may include monosodium glutamate.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Oats supply slow‑releasing carbohydrates that help maintain steady energy levels and promote satiety.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and can aid in blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, and B6 are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Small amount of iron
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood, especially important during physical activity.

items.title: Balanced energy profile
items.content: The mix of carbs and a modest amount of fat provides a quick energy boost without a sharp glucose spike.

items.title: Allergy to nuts or gluten
items.content: Bars may contain nuts, soy, and wheat, posing a risk for individuals with those allergies.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although moderate, the sugar may be a concern for people monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Caloric density if over‑consumed
items.content: Eating multiple bars daily can lead to excess calorie intake.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; those with hypertension should consider the amount.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is convenient to eat straight from the package as a quick snack between meals, can be chopped into yogurt or oatmeal, or used as an energy bite before workouts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 5–7 days to retain the bar’s chewy texture.

chicken-breast-fried-coated-skin-coating.title: Chicken breast, fried, coated, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut taken from the bird's chest. In this form it is first coated in a breading mixture and then fried in oil or a pan, with only the meat portion considered edible while the skin is discarded. It is commonly used in fast‑food items, snacks, and ready‑to‑eat meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The coating usually consists of flour, egg wash and breadcrumbs, giving a crisp crust.
Deep‑frying creates a golden exterior quickly but adds significant calories.
Chicken breast is one of the most popular protein sources worldwide, especially in sports nutrition.
Removing the skin reduces fat content, though some fat remains in the breading.
In many countries the fried chicken breast is served with mayonnaise‑based or tomato‑based sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat in the meat itself
items.content: Without skin, the meat is low in saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, which support bone health and immunity.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The protein is quickly absorbed, making it a good post‑workout option.

items.title: High calorie count from coating
items.content: Breaded and fried preparation adds considerable energy density.

items.title: Possible trans‑fat content
items.content: Using partially hydrogenated oils in the coating can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The breading often contains wheat flour, posing a risk for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may retain pathogens such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breaded chicken breast can be enjoyed as a standalone dish, in salads, sandwiches, or as bite‑size snacks. Pair it with vegetable sides or light sauces to balance the calorie load.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chicken breast in the refrigerator at ≤ 4 °C for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of ≥ 75 °C before consumption.

chicken-drumstick-stewed-skin-not-eaten.title: Chicken drumstick, stewed, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the meat from the thigh portion of a chicken, commonly prepared as stewed dishes. The skin is removed and not consumed, which reduces the fat content. Stewing keeps the meat tender, infuses it with spices, and preserves valuable nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many world cuisines, from Russian to Asian recipes.
Stewing retains more B‑vitamins compared with frying.
The thigh meat contains a good amount of collagen found in connective tissue.
Removing the skin sharply lowers saturated fat levels.
Stewed drumsticks keep well in the fridge for 3‑4 days or can be frozen for longer storage.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Drumsticks provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain B1, B2, B3, B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health, blood formation, and wound healing.

items.title: Low fat when skin is removed
items.content: Without the skin, the calorie and saturated‑fat content is reduced, benefiting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: A rich amino‑acid profile helps maintain and build muscle, especially for active individuals.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked or improperly stored meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Sodium in prepared dishes
items.content: Stewed drumsticks are often seasoned with salt and sauces, increasing sodium intake.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should monitor consumption as it may trigger attacks.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed drumsticks can be served as a main course, added to soups, stews, salads, or used as a filling for pies. When serving, it is advisable to remove bones and any small cartilage fragments.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked drumsticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Kohlrabi is an edible stem vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, related to cabbage, broccoli, and radish. It has a round, slightly flattened shape, light‑green or purple skin, and a crisp, mildly sweet flesh. It is eaten raw, but can also be steamed, sautéed, or added to salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kohlrabi originated as a hybrid of cabbage and radish and was first cultivated around the Mediterranean.
Its vitamin C content exceeds that of oranges while being very low in calories.
Kohlrabi comes in green, purple, or white varieties, with color depending on the cultivar and growing conditions.
In Japan, kohlrabi is often used in traditional dishes such as okonomiyaki and tempura.
It is rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps maintain satiety, and assists in blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Kohlrabi provides few calories, making it a good choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Phytochemicals
items.content: Glucosinolates and polyphenols have anti‑inflammatory and potentially anti‑cancer properties.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: For some people, raw kohlrabi can cause gas and bloating due to complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although rare, individuals allergic to other cruciferous vegetables may react to kohlrabi.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: High vitamin K levels may affect the efficacy of blood thinners such as warfarin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kohlrabi can be eaten raw, thinly sliced into salads, added to smoothies, or used as a crunchy garnish. When cooked, it is often cubed and steamed, roasted, or sautéed to retain its nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kohlrabi in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container; it stays fresh for up to two weeks. For longer storage, wrap it in a damp towel to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Radish (Raphanus sativus) is a crisp, peppery root vegetable of the cruciferous family, native to Asia and Europe. It comes in many shapes and colors, from small round red radishes to long white daikon and black radishes. Radishes are eaten raw in salads and as snacks, pickled, or cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Radishes are one of the fastest-growing vegetables and can be ready to harvest in three to four weeks.
Their peppery heat comes from sulfur compounds called isothiocyanates, also found in mustard and horseradish.
Daikon, a large white radish, is widely used in East Asian cuisine.
Radish leaves and seed pods are also edible.
Radishes belong to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and mustard.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Radishes contain vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Radishes contribute fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Contains potassium and folate
items.content: These nutrients support normal blood pressure and cell function.

items.title: Contains glucosinolates
items.content: These plant compounds, found in cruciferous vegetables, are being studied for their protective activity.

items.title: Low in calories and hydrating
items.content: Radishes are crunchy, low in calories, and high in water.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Radishes, especially raw and in large amounts, may cause gas, bloating, or stomach irritation in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables contain compounds that may affect thyroid function in very large amounts. People with thyroid conditions should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Heartburn
items.content: Very pungent radishes may trigger heartburn in some people.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Radish allergy is uncommon but can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Radishes can be sliced into salads, sandwiches, and tacos, eaten with butter and salt, pickled, roasted, or cooked into soups and stir-fries. Daikon can be grated, simmered, or pickled. Roasting makes radishes milder and slightly sweet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Remove the leaves, which draw moisture, and store radishes in the refrigerator in a bag or container, where they keep for one to two weeks. Radishes can be kept crisp in a bowl of cold water for a short time. Store the leaves separately and use them within a couple of days.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut soup is a traditional dish in Southeast Asian cuisines where peanuts form the base of a thick, aromatic broth. The peanuts give the soup a rich nutty flavor, creamy texture, and a subtle sweetness. It is usually prepared with shelled peanuts, vegetables, spices, and sometimes coconut milk or noodles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts, although they are treated as nuts in cooking.
In Thailand and Vietnam, peanut soup is served as a light lunch or snack.
The peanut sauce used in the soup is often made from roasted peanuts, garlic, and chili for a spicy kick.
Traditional Thai "khao tom" is sometimes enriched with peanut paste to create a thicker consistency.
Peanut soup can be made vegan when no animal broth is used.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, making the soup a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: These fats support cardiovascular health and help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle, nerve, and bone function.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The creamy texture and fiber content help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common food allergens; reactions can be severe.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Peanut soup can be calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones should limit foods high in oxalates.

items.title: Salt and spice levels
items.content: Excessive salt or hot chilies may be unsuitable for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often accompanied by rice, noodles, or fresh herbs. Garnish with crushed peanuts, lime wedges, and cilantro. For a vegetarian version, use vegetable broth instead of meat stock.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months; reheat gently and add fresh herbs before serving.
